paper_title: PREEN: Exemplar-Based Color Style Transfer with Smartphone Editor Presets

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present PREEN (Preset Regression via an Exemplar-based Editor Network), which casts color style transfer as regression onto the 29 parameters of a deterministic image editor. Given a content image and a style reference, PREEN predicts a preset, a vector of editor slider values that is interpretable and editor-consumable, not a raster image. The key obstacle is supervision, since an arbitrary real reference lacks a preset ground truth. We therefore supervise with a style-transfer teacher, whose target looks we invert into the editor's parameter space as pseudo-presets, then pretrain a CLIP-conditioned regressor and refine it with LoRA under an image-level CIELAB loss. On the human-curated PST50 benchmark, PREEN applies the reference's color while preserving structural fidelity, leading the baselines on pixel- and perceptual-fidelity metrics. The preset is compact and predicted at sub-second on-device latency. The low-dimensional subspace also exposes a single inference-time strength knob that traces a continuous default-to-vivid trajectory in one forward pass, with every intermediate state a valid editor preset. A two-axis human study shows that raters prefer the vivid end for matching the reference but the default as a standalone photo, a trade-off the knob spans without retraining.

Introduction Exemplar-based color style transfer, also studied as photorealistic style transfer (PST), is routine operation in modern photo editing. user picks reference image whose look they admire, wanting their own shot recolored to match it (Figure 1). Mainstream academic approaches are pixel-generative, from neural style transfer [13] to diffusion editing [23]. Whatever their quality, they emit rasters with no exposed editing parameters, and the diffusionbased ones add multi-second latency and stochastic sampling that resists deterministic re-editing, an awkward fit for on-device, user-in-the-loop consumer pipelines. An alternative is photo preset transfer [10], predicting Figure 1. PREEN restyles an input toward reference via predicted 29-parameter editor preset (shown at the Vivid strength setting). the parameters of deterministic image editor from the pair (X, ) such that E(X, ) approximates the look of . The output , vector of slider values, is interpretable and compact. Unlike rendered image, it can be stored and re-edited, with no generative model at inference time. The central challenge is supervision. Parametric retouching benchmarks such as MIT-Adobe FiveK [2] and PPR10K [19] provide human-authored target edits, but operate in the auto-enhancement regime without separate style reference. Applying Ppred with our differentiable editor yields pred; the strength knob α scales the presets chroma parameters before editing. PREENs output is compact, human-editable preset rather than rendered image. Flame icons mark the modules updated during training (CLIP only through low-rank adapters), and the snowflake marks the fixed editor. age with reference and matching expert-graded target. The principal prior method [10] sidesteps this by sampling presets, thereby bounding the styles it learns; the only reference-conditioned set with expert-graded targets we know of [7] offers just 50 pairs (PST50) for evaluation. We close this gap with teacher supervision. We propose PREEN (Preset Regression via an Exemplar-based Editor Network). At inference, it maps contentreference pair (X, ) to 29-parameter preset that smartphone editor applies to produce the result (Figure 2). two-stage pipeline trains it. Phase 1 pretrains CLIP-conditioned regressor on large corpus of pseudo-labeled triples recovered from style-transfer teacher. Phase 2 freezes all base weights and trains only low-rank adapters under an image-level CIELAB loss evaluated on the differentiable editor output, addressing the perceptual non-uniformity of Phase 1s parameter-space loss. Our contributions are: (i) teacher-supervised recipe that frees reference-based preset regression from sampledpreset supervision, substituting style-transfer teacher on real references; (ii) strength-interpolation primitive, an inference-time scalar α on the chromaticity parameters that traces continuous default-to-vivid trajectory without rerunning inference; and (iii) two-axis human study surfacing three-way fidelity / style-match / aesthetic divergence across the α trajectory. 2. Related Work 2.1. Photo Preset Transfer Editing photos by predicting the parameters of interpretable white-box operations has long history. Learning-based automatic retouching predicts sequences of editing operations [12], and the same idea recurs in compositing harmonization [15]. Both regress parameters toward fixed goal, enhancement or in-image harmonization, rather than separate style reference. Deep Preset [10] established the reference-conditioned setting we adopt, regressing an editor preset (69 develop controls) from contentreference pair, but its supervision is synthetic by construction. Training references are images re-rendered with sampled presets, so ground-truth preset always exists, but the styles it can learn are confined to that sampled set. The setting has remained underexplored since then; the closest later work, NCST [14], regresses smaller global-only parameter set from reference to perform video grading. We revisit it without sampled-preset supervision: style-transfer teacher on real reference pairs supplies targets we invert into the editors parameter space as pseudo-presets (Section 3). 2.2. Look-Up-Table Stylization separate line maps colors through learned look-up table (LUT), discretized grid over the RGB cube. Imageadaptive 3D LUT [35] and NLUT [3] predict one such grid applied uniformly across the image, and AceTone [22] predicts one from reference with vision-language model. Spatially aware variants blend multiple LUTs per pixel [33], and SA-LUT [7] extends these to spatially adaptive 4D LUT, which we adopt as our teacher. SA-LUT also contributes the human-curated PST50 benchmark used for our evaluation (Section 4.2). Either way, the output is dense grid of 104105 values  (Table 1)  rather than few named sliders, leaving the edit hard for user to inspect or refine. 2.3. Pixel-Generative Stylization large body of work renders stylization through pixel transformations, from classic global color-statistic transfer [29] to AdaIN [13], diffusion-based editing such as SDEdit [23], and recent neural color-style methods including Neural Preset [16], ModFlows [18], and INRetouch [5]. Concurrent work pushes further into generative modeling. SemiNFT [34] casts reference preset transfer as DiffusionTransformer task refined with reinforcement learning for aesthetic perception. These methods emit raster image directly, without exposing user-editable parameters. Neither the LUT nor the pixel-generative family yields an editable preset; we compare experimentally against both families and against Deep Preset, which targets the same task. Table 1. We split the 29 parameters into tone set IL (12: contrast, brightness, exposure, highlights, shadows, per-hue luminance) and chromaticity set Iab (17: temperature, tint, saturation, per-hue hue/saturation). Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup Content images are drawn from OpenImages [17], and style references from the top 20% of the AVA aesthetics database [26] by mean aesthetic score, so references are well-composed, attractively graded photos. We embed every image with CLIP ViT-L/14 [28] and pair each with one of its top-10 nearest references by cosine similarity, so the reference is semantically compatible, not arbitrary. This yields few hundred thousand (X, ) training pairs, supervised by the SA-LUT [7] teacher. The Phase 1 pseudopresets are recovered via Eq. 1. All optimizers are AdamW [20]. Phase 1 inversion (Eq. 1) runs 1,000 steps at learning rate 0.2 per pair with the CIELAB weight λlab = 20, chosen on held-out subset, and small pre-activation magnitude decay (103). Phase 1 regression uses learning rate 3105. Phase 2 trains rank16 LoRA at learning rate 1104, batch size 64, bf16, λ = 102, on an NVIDIA L4 GPU. The augmentation Yaug is random square crop (80100% of the short side) plus horizontal flip. 4.2. User Study Automatic metrics capture fidelity, not perceived quality. We run pairwise preference studies: PREEN Vivid (α = 5) and the default each against (i) Deep Preset ( ˆP ) and (ii) Claude Opus 4.8 predicting the same preset, plus Vivid vs. default (isolating α) and both vs. the SA-LUT teacher. Raters judge style match (closer to the reference) and aesthetic appeal (more pleasing as standalone photo). The VLM opponent uses its guided prompt (Section 4.6). Figure 6 reports PREENs win rates, and the supplementary lists each with its 95% confidence interval. On style match, Vivid wins against every compared preset opponent (Deep Preset 61.6%, Claude 65.7%, PREENs own default 73.4%; pooled 66.9%, [62.2, 71.6]) and roughly ties the teacher itself (44.6%, [36.2, 53.3]), to which the default loses (28.3%). On aesthetic appeal, the ordering inverts. Vivid drops to 43.3% pooled, [38.9, 47.9], with raters favoring the default and Claude as standalone images, yet both PREEN modes are preferred to the teachers fullstrength edit (68.8%/73.8%). This three-way split is the studys central finding. The metrics rank the default highest, human style-match ranks Vivid highest, and standalone aesthetic preference returns to the default. Matches the reference and looks best on its own are different objectives. The α knob spans them without retraining. The default also holds its own. It beats Deep Preset on both axes (61.8% style, [53.0, 70.6]; 67.5% aesthetic, [60.6, 74.0]) and roughly matches Claude Opus 4.8 (52.0%/52.5%) while remaining deterministic and far cheaper. 4.8. On-Device Deployment We export fθ (LoRA merged) to TFLite with 8-bit dynamicrange quantization (INT8 weights, FP32 activations) and benchmark on Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 smartphone (8 CPU threads, median of 20 warm runs). The preset is predicted end-to-end in 283 ms per pair, CPU-only. Latency is dominated by the CLIP backbone (304M of 315M parameters), yet within sub-second UX budget. Quantization preserves accuracy. On PST50, the INT8 artifact scores 24.34/0.915/0.479/0.093/9.02, within 0.3 dB PSNR of Table 1 and matching it on the other four metrics. 5. Discussion and Limitations More than the numbers, PREENs payoff is the form of its output, an interpretable, deterministic preset that an editor consumes directly. Editor Pipeline Details The editor applies the 29 parameters in fixed order typical of consumer smartphone photo editors. Each parameter maps to specific operator and stage (Table S1). Parameters act in [1, 1] and are internally rescaled to the device ranges. Stages 14 operate in RGB, stages 58 on the BT.601 (Rec. 601) luma , and stage 9 in HSL with per-hue Gaussian masks. Every operation is differentiable almost everywhere, so gradients from the Phase 2 image-level loss flow back to Ppred. Table S1 gives the update rule of every stage. The input pixel is = (Xr, Xg, Xb) [0, 1]3, and we write 100 for the (rescaled) parameter of each stage. 2. Full α Sweep Analysis Table S3 reports the full chroma-only α sweep on PST50, extending the two operating points used in the main paper. Toward α 0 the chroma edit is under-applied and the color-facing metrics (HCorr, ab) weaken, and for large α (5, 10) over-saturation degrades every metric. Performance stays close to the α = 1 values for small departures (α [0.5, 2]) and falls off more clearly by α = 3 (PSNR 24.63 23.53, ab 9.07 10.29). We adopt α = 1 as the default operating point. Why chroma-only? Luminance rescale co-saturates tone. Figure S1 contrasts our chroma-only α-scaling with rescaling all 29 parameters (luminance included) on PST50 sample with pronounced warm edit. Chroma-only scaling intensifies the color identity while the tonal anchor stays fixed, so the image keeps similar luminance scale even at α = 10. Rescaling the luminance parameters also co-saturates exposure, brightness, and contrast, driving the tones toward crushed shadows or blown highlights and flattening the photograph as α grows. This motivates restricting the α knob to the chromaticity slice Iab. Does α rotate hue? natural worry is that scaling the chromaticity parameters reorients hue rather than merely intensifying it. We bound the per-channel hue rotation the α knob actually applies (an upper bound, as the per-hue Gaussian weight wh 1), measured over the 7 per-hue channels of all 50 PST50 images. At the default α = 1 no per-hue channel rotates by more than 30 (median 2.1), and even at the Vivid setting (α = 5) only 0.3% do (median 8.9). Pushing to α = 10, twice Vivid, still leaves the median at 14.9 with no channel beyond 60 and only 3.7% past 30. The editors bounded [1, 1] per-hue range thus keeps hue identity largely intact as saturation grows. 3.
